Something happens, then stops, then happens again, then stops again — and this cycle keeps repeating. It never stays continuous.

Think of a flickering street light. It doesn't glow steadily the whole time, and it doesn't stay off the whole time. It switches — on, off, on, off. That light is behaving intermittently.

When you say something happens intermittently, you are really saying three things at once:

  1. It happens — it's present and real.
  2. It pauses — there are clear gaps where it stops.
  3. It comes back — it starts again after each pause.

This repeating cycle of happening → stopping → happening → stopping is the exact signature of "intermittently." If something only happens once and stops, that's not intermittently. If something never stops, that's also not intermittently. The word lives in the middle — the switching back and forth.

• "The Wi-Fi has been working intermittently all day."
    → The connection came on, dropped, came back, dropped again — repeatedly. It never stayed steadily connected.
  • "She cried intermittently throughout the movie."
    → She didn't cry the entire time (that would be "continuously"), and she didn't cry just once. She cried, stopped, cried again, stopped — multiple times across the movie.
  • "It rained intermittently throughout the afternoon."
    → The rain didn't pour for the whole afternoon. It rained for a while, stopped, started again, stopped again — alternating between rain and dry spells.
  • "He checked his phone intermittently during the meeting."
    → Not every single second (that would be "constantly"), and not just once. He checked it a few times with gaps in between.
  • "The old machine works intermittently."
    → It runs for a bit, stops, runs again, stops again — unreliable and unsteady.

No — and this is an important nuance.

"Intermittently" tells you the pattern (stop-start), but it does not tell you how frequent or how rare the occurrences are. Something can happen intermittently but very frequently (on for 30 seconds, off for 10 seconds, on again) — or intermittently but rarely (on for a moment, off for hours, on again briefly). Both are "intermittently."

The word is purely about the nature of the pattern (not continuous, keeps stopping and restarting) — not about how often.
Does "Intermittently" Tell You Whether the Gaps Are Equal?

No — and this is another key nuance.

The pauses between occurrences can be regular (every 10 minutes, like clockwork) or irregular (sometimes 2 minutes, sometimes 45 minutes — completely unpredictable). "Intermittently" covers both. The word only tells you there are pauses — it doesn't promise those pauses are equal.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Understanding the difference from nearby words will make your understanding razor-sharp.

Intermittently vs. Continuously / Constantly
These are direct opposites. "Continuously" means without any pause at all. "Intermittently" means with repeated stopping and restarting.

"The pump ran continuously for 8 hours." → Never stopped.
"The pump ran intermittently for 8 hours." → Kept turning on and off throughout those 8 hours.

Intermittently vs. Occasionally / Sometimes
"Occasionally" and "sometimes" just mean "not always" — they describe low frequency, but they carry no implication of a stopping-and-restarting pattern. "Intermittently" is specifically about that on-off cycling behavior.

"She occasionally reads at night." → She does it from time to time. No emphasis on starting and stopping repeatedly.

"The server crashes intermittently." → It works, crashes, recovers, crashes again, recovers — a clear back-and-forth cycle is happening.

The difference: "occasionally" is about how often; "intermittently" is about the nature of the pattern.

Intermittently vs. Sporadically
These two are the closest pair and are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference: "sporadically" leans toward irregular and unpredictable timing — you can't really anticipate when it will happen next. "Intermittently" is more neutral; it can be predictable or unpredictable.

"Power cuts happen sporadically in this village." → Unpredictable — you never know when.
"Power cuts happen intermittently in this village." → The on-off pattern is clear, but the timing may or may not be predictable.

In everyday usage, most people treat these as synonyms and they'll understand you correctly either way.

Intermittently vs. Periodically
"Periodically" means at regular, somewhat scheduled intervals — there's a sense of rhythm and predictability. "Intermittently" is more neutral and doesn't require regularity.

"The doctor checks your blood pressure periodically." → At planned, regular checkup times.
"The old pipe drips intermittently." → In an uneven, unscheduled way — sometimes more, sometimes less.
The "Feel" of the Word in Real Life

When a fluent speaker hears "intermittently," they picture something unreliable or unsteady — not a total failure, but something that can't be counted on to behave consistently. There's a hint of imperfection or irregularity baked into the word.

This is why "intermittently" appears very naturally in:

  • Technology: "The app crashes intermittently." / "The signal drops intermittently."
  • Weather: "Expect intermittent showers." (Note: "intermittent" is the adjective form of the same word — "intermittently" is the adverb.)
  • Health: "The patient experiences chest pain intermittently."
  • Machines and appliances: "The heating has been working intermittently."
  • Human behavior: "She intermittently loses focus during long tasks."

In all these cases, the thing is neither fully absent nor fully present — it keeps switching.
One-Line Test to Know If "Intermittently" Is the Right Word

Ask yourself: "Is this thing switching between happening and not happening, repeatedly?"

If yes → "intermittently" fits perfectly.
If it happens just once and stops → use "briefly" or "once."
If it never stops → use "continuously" or "constantly."
If it just happens now and then without that clear stop-start cycling → use "occasionally" or "sometimes."

Intermittently means: in a way that keeps stopping and starting again, rather than going on without a break.

The thing is not constant. It is not absent. It exists in an on-off rhythm — whether that rhythm is fast or slow, regular or irregular. That is the full, precise meaning of the word.
